To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

RSA and PEP activity were reciprocally related during rest and stress, and that this relationship was more pronounced for individuals with higher baseline parasympathetically mediated heart rate variability
the SNS and PPS show a reciprocal relationship during the acute stress response, but this reciprocal coupling is moderated by age, gender, race, and baseline levels of RSA.
RSA and PEP show reciprocal coupling during a baseline and in response to an acute stressor.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the coordination of sympathetic (SNS) and parasympthetic (PNS) nervous system activity.
the reciprocal coordination of the sympathetic and parasyymathetic nervous system.
the extent to which the SNS and PPS coordinate activity during rest, stress, and recovery, and how this coordination is moderated by individual characteristics.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

RSA and PEP are reciprocally coordinated during rest and stress, but not during recovery, and that individual differences in RSA and PEP coordination are moderated by sex, age, and baseline ANS activity.
ANS activity is coordinated in a task-dependent manner and is moderated by individual differences in baseline RSA and PPS.
RSA and PEP activity are coordinated in response to a social-evalative stressor, and the extent of this coordination is moderated by age, sex, and baseline ANS functioning.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the ANS is a dynamic system that can be coordinated or decoupled depending on context and individual differences.
ANS responses to a stressor are coordinated, but that the degree of coupling varies across individuals and contexts.

the coordination of sympathetic (PEP) and parasympatic (RSA) activity during rest, stress, and recovery varies across individuals, but that the coordination of SNS and PNs activity may be a core feature of ANS functioning that is not necessarily modulated by the demands of the environment.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the coordination of sympathetic nervous system activity with parasympathic nervous system activity is not uniform across individuals or contexts.
ANS activity is coordinated at the individual level, and that coordination is not fixed but rather varies across individuals and across tasks.

the SNS and PPS are coordinated to a greater extent in response to a social stressor than during rest and recovery, and that individual differences in the extent to, and pattern of, SNS and PPN coordination are evident across these task periods.
